title: Sprout · A screen can open the door
description: An open-source family learning tool for ages 6 months to 3 years. Screens offer a slow prompt; growth happens through responsive care, real objects, play, reading, singing, and outdoor life.

hero.title: A screen can open the door. Growing happens together.
hero.lede: Read a small prompt, put the screen down, and play for a while. Sprout pairs slow parent guidance with printable cards and ordinary moments at home.
hero.meta: v0.0.1 · open source · local network · no ads
hero.sceneLabel: A small television lights up, a seedling grows from the screen, then the television dims and a family returns to real life.

principles.eyebrow: Put the direction on the table
principles.title: Five things, tucked into five seed packets
principles.lede: Each packet is small: open it, read it, then carry the idea back to objects, sounds, and relationships at home.

items.label: Real people
items.title: Responsive people before passive viewing
items.body: What a baby is already noticing deserves a real person who names it, pauses, waits, and responds. A screen is not a substitute for a relationship.
items.evidence: Evidence review 3.1 · video and transfer deficit

items.label: For adults first
items.title: No child-side lessons for 6–17 months
items.body: This stage is for parent guidance: read it, put the device down, and use printed cards, books, and real objects. Co-viewing is off by default at 18–23 months; 24–36 months can also stay screen-free.

items.label: Conversation turns
items.title: Back-and-forth matters more than more input
items.body: Notice what the child is attending to, name it, pause, and respond to a look, gesture, movement, or sound. Then return the idea to daily life.

items.label: Chinese first
items.title: Natural Chinese is the main path; English is optional
items.body: Bilingualism is not a race. Each language needs real, sufficient, natural input; unfamiliar English or recorded audio cannot replace rich conversation.

items.label: Everyday math
items.title: Math starts with quantity, space, and patterns in life
items.body: Touch one, say one, then name the total. Put things in, take them out, sort, and arrange. No flashcards and no correctness score.

stages.title: Six stages, not a race track
stages.lede: Like pencil marks on a doorframe, age is a gentle reference point. Move the paper tag and see what can be brought back into real life.

activities.title: 17 small, finite ways in

home.title: One small server, devices kept in the house
home.lede: The living-room screen does not need to know the wider internet. A Mac, NAS, or small computer serves the player on the home network; a phone opens the parent area only when needed.

points.title: Home network
points.body: The server listens on 4310 by default. The TV, iPad, and parent area use the same family network.

points.title: Data stays at home
points.body: The server stores family data in local SQLite; offline records stay on the current device.

points.title: Six-digit pairing
points.body: The player requests a six-digit pairing code that is valid for 10 minutes; the device token is not printed on the page.

points.title: No server required to start
points.body: The player ships with the sprout.core content pack, so a family can try offline before connecting a home server.

faq.title: Leave the worry at the door; carry less inside

items.q: Will this make children watch more screens?
items.a: It is not designed to extend viewing. Ages 6–17 months get adult guidance only; co-viewing is off by default at 18–23 months; ages 24–36 months can also stay fully offline. Every lesson has a natural ending and an offline next step.

items.q: What about babies younger than six months?
items.a: The core pack starts at 6 months and has no child-side playback path for younger babies. Face-to-face response, floor play, singing, books, and professional child-health guidance come first.
When connected to a server, family data lives in local SQLite on the device running @sprout/server. Offline records stay on the current device.

items.q: Why are there no narration recordings in the repository?
items.a: The public repository does not ship macOS system voices because their license does not allow public redistribution. Without pre-recorded audio, the page uses the browser Web Speech API; a product build can use local or licensed TTS.

items.q: Is it free, and can it be used commercially?
items.a: Code is MIT. Course content is for personal, family, and non-commercial use under the repository's CC BY-NC 4.0 terms; commercial use requires written author permission. Third-party assets keep their own licenses.

No. Sprout is not a medical device, treatment tool, or developmental diagnostic. Milestones are for everyday observation and conversations with professionals. Consult a pediatric or child-health professional when concerns persist or skills regress.

stagePolicies.s1: The grown-up reads the guide; no child-side lesson is shown. Then use cards, books, and real objects together.
stagePolicies.s2: The grown-up reads the guide; no child-side lesson is shown. Then return to real objects and face-to-face play.
stagePolicies.s3: The grown-up reads the guide; no child-side lesson is shown. Then return to real life and outdoor noticing.
stagePolicies.s4: Co-viewing is off by default. If enabled, keep it short and stay with the child; parent guidance alone is always fine.
stagePolicies.s5: Short co-viewing is optional and always with a grown-up. A fully offline path is fine too.
stagePolicies.s6: Short co-viewing is optional and always with a grown-up. A fully offline path is fine too.

s1-t1: Move one printed card slowly and pause to watch the baby's response.
Respond to a look, smile, or sound without asking the baby to imitate.
Offer short tummy-time moments while awake; stop when the baby is tired.
s1-t2: Prefer real faces or family photos and use familiar names.
Tell the baby what you are doing while dressing and name one feature at a time.
Learn the song during the day, then sing one line with the screen off.
s1-t3: Cover only the grown-up's face; keep the baby's nose and mouth clear.
Begin with a large toy partly visible; the grown-up may help reveal it.
Share a shatter-resistant rounded baby mirror without testing self-recognition.
s1-t4: Use one card at a time, name it softly, and pause for a response.
Lift the matching printed card while you sing; do not play background audio.
Learn lullabies during the day, then hum with the screen off at bedtime.
s2-t1: Use real bubbles and large toys to notice changes caused by an action.
Play hide-and-find with a cup large enough to cover a toy; keep the cup still.
An adult prepares and watches every object.
s2-t2: Model the gesture first, then pause for the baby's own response.
Make hello and goodbye part of the same small family ritual.
Learn the melody with the screen off, then sing it and stop whenever needed.
s2-t3: Use foods the baby already eats; do not make the meal longer.
Say two only when both pieces are visible, and say all gone when the plate is empty.
Respect a closed mouth, turning away, or pushing away as a stop signal.
s2-t4: Follow the baby's attention first, then name the real object.
Use the goodnight card book during the day; keep bedtime screen-free.
Support the body during rocking or movement and keep the motion small and slow.
s3-t1: Point to animals with large cards or safe toys.
After copying a sound, pause and wait for the baby's response.
Keep stories gentle and pretend-based; do not create fear or separation.
s3-t2: Name body parts during bathing and dressing.
Let the grown-up model first; watching or doing one small part is enough.
Use slow songs and gentle movement without pulling or forcing touch.
s3-t3: Notice real vehicles from far away, away from roads, wheels, and doors.
Use a low, steady ramp with a large toy vehicle.
Learn the song first, then sing and push a real toy with the screen off.
s3-t4: Use large safe objects, not small foods, to talk about quantity.
Touch one and say one, then name the total.
Use songs for shared rhythm, not for testing number recognition.
s3-t5: Show clothing while dressing and invite a hand or foot movement.
Use a routine card to preview socks, shoes, and a hat.
Learn the handwashing song first; stay within reach near water.
s3-t6: Follow the baby's gaze and name a tree, flower, bird, or cloud.
Listen to rain indoors first; avoid standing water and unsafe surfaces.
Imitate a tree, bird, or rabbit without asking for jumping or balance.
s4-t1: Look for one color at home.
Offer free scribbling without asking for color naming or a rainbow.
s4-t2: Notice outlines with round objects and shape cards.
Model a shape-matching toy without forcing it into place.
Build a low tower on the floor; try again if it falls.
s4-t3: Touch one and say one, then name the total.
Count spoons and shoes, not small foods.
Play stop-and-go gently, without elimination or breath-holding.
s4-t4: Look at feeling cards and practise asking for help when calm.
When a real feeling arrives, put the device down and protect safety first.
Respect the child's wish for a hug or breathing space while staying close.
s4-t5: Adults help brush twice a day and use only a rice-sized amount of toothpaste.
Stay within arm's reach around water.
Wash with soap for at least 20 seconds, then rinse and dry.
A song is not a cleaning timer; keep the screen off during care.
s4-t6: Compare two objects from the same kind at a time.
Begin by nesting two large cups, then add a third if interested.
Use sitting or supported standing; do not ask for jumping or tiptoeing.
s5-t1: Sort large objects with clear main colors into red and blue.
Model one object, then wait for the child's attempt.
Say what feature you are sorting by; perfect accuracy is not the goal.
s5-t2: Begin counting with one or two large objects.
Name the total after counting; do not test numeral recognition.
Use counting songs as shared play, not a quiz.
s5-t3: Say swims in water and flies in the sky; do not say birds live in the sky.
Read animal books together and never approach or feed wild animals.
Pandas can climb trees; keep the child's pretend play on the ground.
s5-t4: Model taking turns without forcing a child to give up a treasured toy.
Ask how the child feels without sorting feelings into right and wrong.
Use polite words inside real help and repair.
s5-t5: Use dolls and open boxes to say in, out, up, and down.
Do one step first, then invite the child to give the grown-up a direction.
Stay off furniture, out of closed boxes, and away from climbing play.
s5-t6: Notice local weather; a book is fine when snow is not part of daily life.
Choose clothing for the real temperature, not only the weather icon.
A rain song is a wish, not a way to stop the rain.
s6-t1: Use socks and towels to make two complete repeats.
Take turns clapping and stamping softly; sitting is an option.
A three-part pattern is optional; return to two alternating items if needed.
s6-t2: Touch one and say one, then name the total; do not test numeral reading.
Start with one to three large objects; adults can support four or five.
Line up same-sized objects one-to-one, then talk about more and fewer.
s6-t3: Sit securely while trying one clothing step; an adult checks comfort and safety.
Use a two-step plan: first this, then that.
Do not rush toileting; clean carefully after toilet or diaper care.
Praise the specific attempt and help promptly when needed.
s6-t4: Use dolls to practise goodbye and a promised pickup without creating real separation.
Let the child say what feels worrying and name a trusted teacher for help.
Name real objects; follow the preschool's own pickup and belongings rules.
Model polite words without forcing hugs or public English.
s6-t5: Offer a varied everyday diet; keep sweets occasional and never force a clean plate.
Lower the movement challenge, steady the body, and do not turn balance into a test.
Learn bedtime songs during the day and keep bedtime screen-free.
Keep meals screen-free and supervise water, toothbrushing, and lamps.
s6-t6: Adults handle seeds and soil while children observe a real seedling.
Talk about day and night at clear times; the moon can also appear during the day.
Look at the same tree repeatedly and allow local seasons to differ.
Do not look at the sun, climb windowsills, or go out in dangerous weather.

lessonVehiclesEn.intro: Read this first. An adult chooses a safe place to notice vehicles. Name one vehicle at a time. When none are nearby, use the large printed cards. There is no need to go to a road or water.
tips: Name one vehicle that is actually in front of you.
Describe first, then invite your child to look or listen.
Use English as a short label, never instead of rich conversation.
lessonVehiclesEn.why: Follow what the child is already noticing. Name it, pause, and wait for a response. Real conversation matters more than vehicle video.
steps: Choose a safe place away from traffic and parking entrances.
Point to one vehicle and say its name slowly.
Pause for a look, movement, or sound. Keep your voice small.
At home, choose one printed card at a time.
lessonVehiclesEn.safety: Stay with the child. Keep away from roads, rails, wheels, doors, and water. Do not use loud recorded vehicle sounds. Close windows and keep away from windowsills and furniture.
lessonVehiclesEn.question: What sound did you hear?
lessonVehiclesEn.easier: Look at one card at home. The adult names it and makes a soft sound.
lessonVehiclesEn.harder: From a safe place, notice two vehicles and name each one.
phrases: This is a car, beep beep.
We stay in a safe place.
